description: exp3 iter_1 c4: lambda varies per judgement (logit-normal, 9-node GH) on range_limited incumbent: +1.55 MAP, sd .73 not collapsing; width/Erlang/parity/kind-reliability all collapse
metadata:
  type: project
---
exp3 iter_1/candidate_4 (2026-11-01) is variable_rule_range_expectation. The incumbent range_limited_rule_familiar_strays has a fixed lambda; here logit(lambda) ~ N(mu, sd), and the membership posterior is averaged over 9 Gauss-Hermite nodes on the (sets, concepts, K) log-joint.
- MAP ll: -3319.24 vs -3320.79 for the incumbent. lambda_sd = .73.
- Train p_yes RMSE vs the incumbent: .007. Smoke fit 57 s. Check OK.
- It does NOT close the critique narrow_rule_inhull_nonmember_span_contrast: narrow in-span non-member yes is .52 observed vs .41 predicted. Nothing tried moves that number.
Tried on the incumbent, all at MAP, none useful:
- interval width^-gamma prior: gamma .03, ll +0.06.
- Erlang interval prior: ll -4.1.
- separate parity-rule weight: beta -.09, ll +0.25.
- separate range reliability: +0.42.
Odd residual: 16,26,96 → 67 gets 5/5 yes while 61, 64, 65 and 69 get 0/5 (probably the "6 7" meme, which the models cannot express).
**How to apply:** prior *variability* (integrated per judgement) is a lever that does not collapse, unlike prior *shape* changes. See [[normative-distortions-collapse]] and [[range-limited-rule-familiar-strays]].
---
name: cluster-cued-range-salience
description: exp3 iter_1 c2: range prior × exp(beta·(1-span/99)) on range_limited incumbent, beta≈.47, +1.8 MAP; Erlang/width priors fail on the narrow-span critique
metadata:
  type: project
---
exp3 iter_1/candidate_2 (2026-11-01), cluster_cued_range_salience. The critique narrow_rule_inhull_nonmember_span_contrast is driven by narrow odd-only sets (31,3,1,15: obs .93 vs pred .53; 63,23,43; 73,35,53,59; 37,57). There people accept the evens inside the span. Wide-span sets were calibrated.
- Erlang range-size prior: ll −4 (sigma→39). Width power s^-γ: γ→.03, a tie. Range-size priors cannot fix this.
- Data-dependent range salience, log range prior + beta·tight: tight = 1−span/99 with n=1 → 0 gave +1.8 MAP (−3318.97); the narrow-span pred rose .41→.44. A log-span version gave +0.8; counting n=1 as tight gave +0.7.
- Training RMSE vs the incumbent is .011. Check OK; smoke fit 24 s.
**How to apply:** clustering cues help a little. A remaining gap could come from restricted rules ("odd within range") penalising in-span evens. See [[range-limited-rule-familiar-strays]] and [[normative-distortions-collapse]].
---
name: typical-width-magnitude-bands
description: exp3 iter_1 c0: Erlang width prior on ranges (rule_count base) loses 5 MAP ll (sigma≈19); exponential loses 9; uniform per-range prior already favours narrow
metadata:
  type: project
---
exp3 iter_1/candidate_0 (2026-11-01), typical_width_magnitude_bands. It targets the critique narrow_rule_inhull_nonmember_span_contrast. For in-span rule non-members, the incumbent's yes-rate is too low on narrow spans (obs .52 vs pred .41) and right on wide spans (.22 vs .21). The narrow gap comes mostly from 31,3,1,15 (2, 4, 16 said yes) and from 66,78.
- Erlang(size; sigma) / (101 - size) per range, on rule_count_familiar_strays: MAP ll -3326.7 against -3321.8, sigma 19. The narrow-span prediction only moves .41 → .43.
- An exponential width density does worse: -3330.6, sigma 37.
- Uniform per-range priors already imply a size mass ∝ (101 - s), so width priors cannot close the gap. Submitted anyway; smoke fit 31 s, check OK.
- Implementation: run_count tables (sets, runs, 100) as data, with pt.dot against the weighted size^-j inside the model.
See [[compressed-number-line-ranges]], [[range-limited-rule-familiar-strays]].
---
name: range-limited-rule-familiar-strays
description: exp3 iter_0 c4: rule∩range concepts on rule_count_familiar_strays; rho≈0.095 (free, not collapsing), +1.0 MAP, RMSE .009; equal rule prior makes it (set,subset,size) tables; p_yes eval gotcha
metadata:
  type: project
---
exp3 iter_0/candidate_4 (2026-11-01), range_limited_rule_familiar_strays. Motivated by the critique clean_rule_member_inside_minus_outside_hull (obs 0.18 vs null 0.10). Restricted rules = proper non-empty member blocks of each rule, weighted by # ranges cutting them (gap products), prior lambda_0*rho/(45*5050). rho_logit ~ N(-2,1). MAP ll -3320.79 vs incumbent -3321.79; rho 0.095 (unlike exp2, where it collapsed to the prior, see [[range-restricted-rules]]). Brute force check exact.
Speed: because rules are equally weighted, sum over rules into count tables, then fold the size axis in prepare_observed (count @ size^-j → [set|cell,16,5]) and multiply by e_sub*c. With dense (cells,16,100)*sub_size_lik the smoke fit took 236 s; folded, 21 s.
Gotcha: to evaluate p_yes at a MAP point, use pytensor.function(value_vars, model.replace_rvs_by_values([p_yes])[0]). A raw pytensor.function on p_yes samples the RVs, and compile_fn with a dict mis-maps. Both give garbage.

"""Cluster-cued range salience.

Hypothesis: which kind of program comes to mind depends on how the examples look.

I wrote the candidate **`min_max_bounded_range`**, and the admission check prints `OK` (31 s smoke fit, finite log-likelihood of −3322.1). It improves the fit a little and predicts differently from the existing models, but it closes only a small part of the gap the critique flagged.

**Hypothesis:** people take the smallest and largest example as the limits of a possible program. So for sets of two or more examples, the range from the lowest to the highest example comes to mind much more readily than any other range. Everything else is the same Bayesian concept learner as `range_limited_rule_familiar_strays`. The change adds one free parameter: how much extra prior weight that one range gets.

**Results (best-fitting parameters):**
- **Fit:** log-likelihood −3319.10, against −3320.79 for the base model and −3318.97 for `cluster_cued_range_salience`.
- **The boost stays real:** that range gets about 7× the prior of an ordinary range, rather than shrinking to nothing.
- **Different predictions:** on the training data, its per-trial "yes" probabilities differ from the base by 0.009 and from the cluster-cued model by 0.012 (RMSE). The near-duplicate cutoff is 0.002, though I didn't run the formal novelty check on the novelty pool.
- **Effect on the critique:** for rule non-members inside narrow spans, people say yes 0.578 of the time on my count. The base predicts 0.407, this model 0.430 and the cluster-cued model 0.436. Changes to the range prior keep moving this by only about 0.02.

**What the data suggests:** much of the fill-in looks local, at non-members right next to an example (17 and 19 after 16; 78–88 after 77, 89; 7, 11, 13, 15 after 4, 16, 12). The 31, 3, 1, 15 → 2, 4, 16 responses may be a powers-of-2 association. Neither pattern is something a range-prior change can produce. I saved these notes to memory.
